1.title: The Product Owner
1.text: Welcome to Module 4: The Product Owner. In the last module you met the whole Scrum Team. Now we look closely at one accountability: the person responsible for the value of the product. You will learn what that means, why it must be one person, and where the Product Owner's authority ends and collaboration begins.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. State what the Product Owner is accountable for. Explain why the Product Owner is one person, giving at least two reasons. Show how the Product Owner keeps authority while collaborating with the Developers and stakeholders. Place the Product Owner in each event. And spot the traps: committees, assigned work, sizing, and cancelling a Sprint.

1.title: Case Check-In: Everyone Wants Their Item First
1.text: At RideLoop, Grace Whitfield and the Station Crew each want their item at the top of the Product Backlog. Instead of talking to Maya, both go straight to a Developer. Ben is asked to add an item to the Sprint right away. Ben looks at you for help. You are the Scrum Master, and the question in your mind is simple: who decides the order of the Product Backlog? This module gives the answer.

1.title: Accountable for the Value of the Product
1.text: The Product Owner is accountable for "maximizing the value of the product" that the Scrum Team creates. How that is done varies widely across organizations, teams and people. The Guide does not fix the method; it fixes who decides. The decisions are visible in the Product Backlog and in the Increment shown at the Sprint Review. The work may be delegated, but the accountability stays with the Product Owner. In the earlier edition, you will find the words sole person responsible. Delegating never transfers accountability.

1.title: Product Backlog Management
1.text: The Product Owner is accountable too for managing the Product Backlog well, in four parts. Develop and clearly communicate the Product Goal. Create and clearly communicate the Product Backlog items. Order the items. And make sure everyone can see and understand the Product Backlog. The Product Owner may do this work personally, or delegate it to others. Either way, the accountability stays.

1.title: The Product Owner Across the Guide
1.text: Where else does the Guide give the Product Owner a role? In Sprint Planning, the Product Owner prepares attendees, puts forward the value, discusses items with the Developers, who select them, and helps shape the Sprint Goal. During the Sprint, the Product Owner negotiates scope with the Developers when the work turns out different, always protecting the Sprint Goal. The Product Owner alone can cancel a Sprint, and only when the Sprint Goal is obsolete. At the Review, the Product Owner discusses progress, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted.

1.title: One Person, Not a Committee
1.text: The Guide puts it plainly: "one person, not a committee." That person may represent the needs of many stakeholders, but those who want to change the Product Backlog must try to convince the Product Owner. And for this to work, the whole organization must respect the Product Owner's decisions. The diagram shows the flow of influence. At RideLoop, that means Grace and the Station Crew make their case to Maya, and Ben points them to Maya. If an exam option has a committee, a vote or a manager deciding the order of the Product Backlog, it is wrong.

1.title: Why One Person?
1.text: Why one person? The learning objective asks for at least two reasons, and these go beyond the Guide. Clear accountability: one person answers for the value, so success and failure have an owner. Faster decisions: the Developers get one answer instead of a negotiation. One ordered Product Backlog, without competing priorities. No deadlock, because conflicting interests are balanced by one decision maker. And one voice for the team and the stakeholders. Stakeholders advocate; the Product Owner decides.

1.title: Authority and Collaboration
1.text: How does the Product Owner keep authority while collaborating? The Product Owner decides the content and order of the Product Backlog, and develops the Product Goal. The Developers decide the sizing, select the items for the Sprint in discussion with the Product Owner, and decide how the work is done. The whole Scrum Team shapes the Sprint Goal. Scope changes inside the Sprint are negotiated between the Product Owner and the Developers. The Product Owner can help with trade-offs on sizing, but does not set the sizes.

1.title: The Product Owner in the Events
1.text: The Product Owner is a member of the Scrum Team, so the Product Owner takes part in the events. In Sprint Planning, the Product Owner prepares attendees, proposes value and discusses items. The Daily Scrum is the Developers' event, so the Product Owner is not required there. If the Product Owner is actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they take part as a Developer. At the Sprint Review and the Retrospective, the Product Owner takes part as a member of the team.

1.title: What the Product Owner Is Not
1.text: It also helps to know what the Product Owner is not. Not a committee. Not the person who assigns work or decides how it is built. Not the person who sizes the items. Not the Scrum Master's manager, because there are no hierarchies in the Scrum Team. And not a gatekeeper who approves every Increment: the Guide gives no such role, and work counts when it meets the Definition of Done.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. One person: never a committee, a board or a vote. Accountable, not necessarily doing: the work may be delegated. Stakeholders convince; they do not command. The Developers size the items, select them for the Sprint, and decide how. Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint. And when several Scrum Teams work on one product, they share one Product Owner, one Product Backlog and one Product Goal. The Product Owner is part of the Scrum Team.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The Product Owner is accountable for the value of the product and for Product Backlog management. It is one person, for clear accountability and one order. The Product Owner has authority over the content and order of the Product Backlog. The Developers size, select and decide how. Scope is negotiated without harming the Sprint Goal. And only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Grace's steering group proposes that three managers jointly act as Product Owner, so that everyone's interests are covered. What should the Scrum Master explain? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The Product Owner is a single person, who may represent the needs of many stakeholders. The managers make their case to that person. A casting vote or a weekly meeting does not restore single accountability.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Under pressure from Grace, Maya wants the Developers to size every item as small, so that more items fit in the Sprint. What is correct? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Sizing belongs to the Developers. Maya can help them understand trade-offs, for example by simplifying an item, but Maya cannot dictate the size. Neither the Scrum Master nor a stakeholder vote sets sizes.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Midway through a Sprint, Lakeshore Transit decides to replace the unlock flow with a partner's solution, so the Sprint Goal is obsolete. Who has the authority to cancel the Sprint? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The Product Owner alone can cancel a Sprint, and only when the Sprint Goal has become obsolete. Others may raise the concern with the Product Owner.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which is a reason why the Product Owner is one person and not a committee? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. One person answers for the value and produces one order of the Product Backlog. Stakeholders can still share their needs and try to convince the Product Owner, so option C is wrong.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which list describes what effective Product Backlog management includes? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. It covers developing and communicating the Product Goal, creating and communicating items, ordering them, and making sure everyone understands the Product Backlog. The other lists describe the Developers and the Scrum Master.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. A single person, not a group. Question two: D. The Developers size the items. Question three: A. The Product Owner alone can cancel a Sprint. Question four: D. Clear accountability and one ordered Product Backlog. Question five: C. Goal, items, order and transparency. That completes Module 4. Next, Module 5 covers the Scrum Master.
